title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake video or image of Australian financial figures in a fabricated interview promoting an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The scam relied on impersonation through synthetic media rather than on the AI system making false claims itself. The deployment failure was that the fraudulent content reached audiences without verification that the people depicted had actually made these statements or endorsed this platform.

What enabled this scam to spread is not established in the reporting. Whether the synthetic media was posted directly by scammers to social platforms, whether it appeared in ads, or how it first reached readers is unknown. A human check at any point—by a platform moderating uploads, by a viewer checking the platform's license, or by verifying the statements with the depicted individuals—would have stopped it.

This is confirmed as part of a broader pattern rather than an isolated incident. Australian authorities report that AI-generated impersonations of public figures promoting fraudulent investments have become common enough to warrant formal warnings, though the prevalence of this specific attack method compared to others is not established.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler was recently removed from the internet. The fabricated interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This incident exemplifies a rising trend of AI-generated investment scams that the Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Research released by ASIC shows that scammers use deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to create convincing but fraudulent investment opportunities.

Last year, ASIC took down 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated public figure, followed by other politicians and financial experts including Alan Kohler. ASIC warns consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing. The regulator advises people not to trust polished content or familiar branding alone and recommends checking company legitimacy independently through ASIC's free public registers.
